body_ar: لا زيارة القبور إذا كانت على الوجه الشرعي فهي مندوبة تذكر الآخرة لقول النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم:«كنت نهيتكم عن زيارة القبور فزوروها فإنها تذكركم الآخرة » و قال صلى الله عليه وسلم: « كنت نهيتكم عن زيارة القبور فزوروها و لا تقولوا هجرا » و الهجر الكلام القبيح أي غير المأذون به شرعا و قد سبقت آداب الزيارة الشرعية في عدد من الدروس بالإمكان أن تراجع في الأشرطة و بيان الفرق بين الزيارة السنية و الزيارة المبتدعة.
body_en: No. Visiting graves, when it is done in the manner the revealed law allows, is recommended (mandūb): it brings the hereafter to mind. This is on account of the words of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him: 'I had forbidden you from visiting graves; now visit them, for they remind you of the hereafter.' And he said, peace and blessings be upon him: 'I had forbidden you from visiting graves; now visit them, but do not speak hujr.' And hujr is foul speech — that is, speech not permitted in the revealed law. The proprieties of the lawful visit have already been given in a number of lessons, which can be reviewed on the recordings, together with the explanation of the difference between the visit that accords with the sunnah and the visit that is an innovation.

flags.context: the Sheikh's ruling on visiting graves
flags.note: The Sheikh uses a precise five-rulings term and it is fixed in the glossary as 'recommended'. Note what the pairing does: the title asks whether visiting graves is FORBIDDEN, and the answer is that it is RECOMMENDED — two opposite ends of the five-rulings scale. Any looseness in the English here would misstate the ruling, and 'a confirmed sunnah' would raise it a grade beyond what he said.

flags.arabic: إذا كانت على الوجه الشرعي … بيان الفرق بين الزيارة السنية و الزيارة المبتدعة
flags.context: the condition on which the whole ruling depends, and the cross-reference that would explain it
options: render faithfully and mark that the condition is never explained here
supply the proprieties from elsewhere in the corpus
flags.note: CRITICAL FOR DISPLAY. The ruling of 'recommended' is conditional throughout on the visit being 'in the manner the revealed law allows', and the Sheikh explicitly declines to set out that manner here, referring the questioner instead to recorded lessons. The record therefore gives a ruling and withholds the condition that governs it. Nothing has been supplied from elsewhere. The site should carry the caveat, and this is also a concrete instance of the corpus-wide problem that the substance is in the audio: the proprieties exist only 'on the recordings'.

flags.arabic: و لا تقولوا هجرا … و الهجر الكلام القبيح
flags.context: the second report and the Sheikh's own gloss of hujr
options: keep hujr in transliteration and give the Sheikh's gloss after it, as done here
translate hujr directly as 'foul speech' and drop the transliteration
flags.note: The word is kept because the Sheikh immediately glosses it himself, and dropping it would make his gloss read as a tautology in English. His gloss goes beyond the lexical sense: he defines hujr as speech 'not permitted in the revealed law', which is what makes the report bear on the difference between a lawful and an innovated visit. Both layers have been kept. He gives no narrator, collection or grading for either report and none has been supplied.
